It’s supposed to be somewhere in the Kennedy Center as founding artists, but I haven’t been able to find it. She went for that occasion to Teddy Kennedy’s house for that dedication and the reception. She went to Bill Clinton, President Clinton, invited us to play at the…
You played for the king of Morocco?
Yes.
King Hassan, the II.
Hassan was there, and boy, his daughter was there with some jewels that you wouldn’t believe. And his son, they are handsome kids…
This was in 1992, if I’m not mistaken.
Yes, just a year before he passed. He was supposed to get the Brothers to come to Morocco but he passed before…
Just to let you know, the tunes on with “The Blue Necklace,” “Three Little Feelings”…

“The Blue Necklace” is the other one that was part of that score. “Three Little Feelings” was John Lewis’s composition from way back, and I loved it. It was performed, too on his last appearance at the Lincoln Center by the Orchestra. It was touching, I’m telling you.
Yes, I was there. The other album Space, which I thought was interesting because this came out around the time of 2001: A Space Odyssey. I always wondered, was there a connection?
No, “Space” I think was a part of that score…
Part of “Kemek”?
I think so.
Oh! Okay.
I think it was part of that score.
Now, for those of us who don’t know, what was “Kemek”? And it’s spelled K-E­ M-E-K.
E-K, was it?
Right.

It was a movie that we were doing the soundtrack for. The day that the film was finished, the director died or something, and it was never released. So, somebody died after we worked very hard on that melodrama. It was another one of those “who done its.”
It was a psychological thing. Did it have kind of a, not an LSD angle, but something to do with psychotropic drugs?

I don’t know. It was the first use of this so-called fishbowl eye [lens] that took the photograph from above, and it gave a certain illusion, dimension, like an overhead shot of this person going out of it. We never even did get to see the whole movie. It was completed, and the one piece that you referred to is “Plastic Dreams.”
Actually no, I’m talking about “Space” with “Visitor from Venus,” “Visitor from Mars”…
Oh, that wasn’t part of that.
That was another part of the Apple.
That was just a part of, John Lewis wrote some pieces that were far out.
What I notice about this is two things, I think that was one of the first MJQ recordings where electric piano was used, and number two, the liner notes…
Was it electric piano or harpsichord?
It may have been the harpsichord. I’m sorry. On the liner notes, they seem to be the most political liner notes you guys have because there were anti-war feelings in the liner notes.

I don’t know who did the notes, but when you engage somebody to do liner notes and their descriptions of the music are not necessarily the intent of the composer, it’s another incident of trying to verbalize an intangible. You know what I mean? What label they put on it… I don’t know. I do have the album here somewhere. You read all these notes, I probably never read the liner notes.
[laughs] What you were referring to is the soundtrack from Kemek turned out was Plastic Dreams, now you gotta tell me, what was the deal with the album cover? Who thought of that?
Who did it? Yeah, I don’t know, some artist brought it in and it was approved.
And for those of us who can’t see it, the liner notes or collage of a nude woman with…
Well, not exactly nude. It’s an artistic interpretation. It had some phony breasts there, which was “Plastic Dreams.” It just went with the (title?).
Not something you would expect from the composed Modern Jazz Quartet
[laughs].

Well, the album cover, I forget who did it, but it was an artist’s concept of “Plastic Dreams,” which was accepted. It was a little risqué, but we are human beings and we’re not above…life. What is that on the other album cover, Jasmine Tree? That’s a serpent of some kind. I don’t know if it had anything to do with the music. There’s another album cover there wit a slice of bread. So, album covers are artistic…
Open to interpretation.
[Laughs] Yeah, artistic, whatever the artist deems appropriate.
[End of disc 4]

This is tape number three of the Percy Heath interview for the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History project. My name is Eugene Holley. The engineer is Sven Abow. We’re here at the great home of Mr. Percy Heath in Montauk, New York, July 23, 2001.
The modest home. The modest home in paradise.

Right, coming down to the home stretch. Mr. Heath, the MJQ, in addition to being four great musicians, you guys actually had distinct non-musical duties in the group. Describe what they were, and describe what yours was.

In the formation of the Modern Jazz Society Inc. and then the formation of the Quartet as an entity of that along with the publishing company and proposed presenting of concerts and other artists, within the Quartet it was asked why was John Lewis the musical director. It was John Lewis’s concept of the music, which was the Modern Jazz Quartet and as such, he was the musical director. However, some contributions of some of the compositions in the repertoire were compositions of Milt Jackson, and he also rearranged “The Watergate Blues,” which was my composition. In general, in fact, all of the music was arranged at least, even Milt Jackson’s so-called composition, his musical lines that he wrote on the vibraharp, which were single note lines, generally. The harmonic part sometimes was supplied by John Lewis and in other cases on Milt Jackson’s albums, it was supplied by Jimmy Heath, who arranged compositions on several of Milt Jackson’s albums. So, that was John’s job, musical director, composer and author. He also did most of the announcements. They were split up at concerts between

he and Milt. Connie Kay was dubbed the “Minister of Transport” by W. Talbot in England because Connie used to arrange the tickets and hotel reservations, which is another part of the story of pioneering that I’ll add on to after I explain these different positions. My position at that time, and for the first twenty-two years without interruption, was to collect the money in every country and pay the salaries and do the banking. I was the “Minister of Finance” in that respect, to quote W. Talbot’s description of Connie’s job. Milt Jackson was supposed to be sort of public relations. He would do interviews, and we found that Jackson most of the time was talking about Jackson on these interviews, so we had to throw in a few words about the Quartet most of the time. Milt was like that. By us growing out of the Milt Jackson Quartet, he never really realized that it was not still the Milt Jackson Quartet, but that was forgivable because of the great artist he was and most of the improvisation, even though it was underlined by John Lewis’s accompaniment, single note line or whatever, the one fed off of the other. That was the integral part of the Quartet. That’s the four members’ responsibilities as a partnership. Of course, later on, I was relieved of the duties of taking care of the money ‘cause I turned that over to Milt’s wife, Sandra, and she took care of all that bookkeeping and stuff that I had to do for all those years, which was quite a relief. I could just be the bass player again. The construction of the Quartet with those jobs, it sort of justified the equal pay and the partnership that evolved, which was quite unique at the time. I think the Glen Gray Casa Loma Orchestra was also like a partnership, and Glen Gray’s name was just out there, but it acted as a corporate entity too.

I think the only thing that’s more astounding than your tenure with the Modern Jazz Quartet is the fact that you only record, if I’m not mistaken, there’s only one of your own compositions that you recorded with the Modern Jazz Quartet, “The Watergate Blues.” When did you write that?

I was really annoyed about all this business about scandal and whatnot in the presidency at that time and the denial of being implicated, which all led to the downfall of President Nixon. It was really something that they did in Washington anyhow, spying on each other. Politics is a dirty game. At that time, it was so much emphasis put on this little case of spying and the cost of the presidency and a lot of other scandal that came out at that time. My exasperation when Mr. Ford pardoned Mr. Nixon, it was really upsetting to me that all this so-called crime could be made, in one stroke of a pen, forgotten. Some of the lyrics to it are quite profound. There’s not just the melody, which was a little different and became popular for the Heath Brothers repertoire. The Quartet had a TV show in Boston on which Mr. Ehrlichman had just gotten out of jail for his participation…
The Quartet was on a TV show?
On a TV show that he was on in Boston, and I had the audacity to give Mr. Ehrlichman a copy. Was it Ehrlichman or the other guy?
Halderman?

No, it was Ehrlichman. He got out of jail and we were on the same TV show in Boston, and I said, “Here John, if you record this we’ll both get rich,” and I handed him a copy of it [laughs]. I don’t think he liked it very much, but there’s some words in there, “On the next election day/It’s Mr. Ford who will have to pay/because of something with the Watergate Blues,” so he was not reelected. A lot of people didn’t think he should’ve pardoned Mr. Nixon after all that expose. But there are some very clever words there that match the rhythm of the melody. Like my father used to say, “They’re a bunch of educated fools,” and one of the verses says, “They read an awful lot of books and spent a lot of time in school…” something about crooks, and then the other line says, “They’re a bunch of educated fools” with the melody. These words just came to me, I haven’t seen it in a long time, but it’s not bad. There are about six different verses of that.

The other group that you were involved with was, of course, the Heath Brothers, and just give me kind of an origin. You’ve always played with your brothers. Tell me how the group came together and what were your high points of the group?

Well, we got together when the Quartet broke up and I had an opportunity to join my brothers in a group. ‘Cause, Jesus, 22 years I had devoted to this music and all of a sudden, the group is no more. I said, “I have to make the best of it,” and now I have a chance to get together with my brothers, who were successful in their own right doing other things. We had been associated on several records, one of Tootie’s and three or four of Jimmy’s albums, the brothers had come together and played on. You know the one of Tootie’s that’s called Kwanzaa?
Mid-70s, I believe.

Yeah, so anyhow, we had been associated together on recordings, but now we had the chance to play together in a group. I don’t know, I might have been instrumental in securing this contract with Columbia, and we did four albums for them, which were really good albums. I hope they come out again sometime.
I don’t mean to cut you off, but I wanna get to the point about Strata East. I don’t really remember the Strata East one. The early members of the band were Stanley Cowell, Tony Purrone…

Yeah, it was a quartet at first. In fact, the first time the Heath Brothers played, we played in Pescara, just the three of us. No piano. That was on a festival in (Pescara). We were booked as the Heath Brothers, and we played just the three of us. Then we had the opportunity to record on Strata East label, which was like a musician-owned label. I have a copy of it, I’ll show you there. It’s a picture of our mother and father that’s in my studio that’s on the album cover, and it’s called Marchin’ On, with them in their Elks uniforms. They both had passed by the time we got to play together, but they were very proud of us

individually. When Tootie was with Lester Young in Philly, Pop would go up and brag about, “that’s my boy!” My father was really proud of us, especially when Lt. Heath came home, and soldiers would pop into attention and salute me from across the street. He had great pride in that achievement, so throughout our whole life, they were really beautiful people, my parents. Exceptional. Like I said earlier, we had the support of them in our musical careers that other families didn’t give to their siblings that wanted to pursue a jazz career. That opportunity came for us to be together, and we put out that one record. I think we only printed 2,000, but I got a copy of a CD that somebody else put out recently. It’s been put out on CD now, and in Japan somebody picked it up. But that initial album, on one complete side was the suite that Jimmy wrote for Billy Higgins called “Smilin’ Billy.” It had several movements, and with the joining of Stanley Cowell, who was the president and part owner of that label, Strata East, he played the kalimba. He had a couple of octaves of keys on it. Have you heard that album? Stanley played the kalimba very melodically, and he had his own tuning. Stanley Cowell is a remarkable pianist, too and a professor also for all these years at Lehman College up there. The Brothers are gonna go down there to Baltimore or somewhere he presents…
Prince George’s Community College?

He presents concerts down there. The Brothers are going down there, and we’re gonna be joined by Stanley on piano for that occasion. The Heath Brothers Quartet, I’ve given you some posters to show where we appeared in several places. And like I said before, as soon as we got to going good with the Heath Brothers and those four albums out on Columbia and the two on Island, we were just going good, it takes time to build and organization, then…
Then MJQ reforms.

Here comes Jackson back and we did another ten years. Now we’re together. On many occasions now that’s the only jobs I’m taking outside of two individual jobs that I had, the one with John Lewis at Lincoln Center and a couple with Cedar Walton and Curtis Fuller and the all-star group with Lou Hayes on drums, I made a few gigs with them. Otherwise, I’m doing something out here in Montauk with Hal McKusick a couple of times a year and more local. With this organization that I’m the president of, the Montauk Artists’ Association, we acquired the train station out here in Montauk as a depot gallery, and we’re in the midst of a fundraiser the 3rd and 4th of August at the clubhouse of the golf course out here, the Downs in Montauk.
You’re being very modest, but this is the first Montauk Jazz Festival and there’s a tribute to you.
That’s okay, but the purpose is to rehabilitate the upstairs of the train station. It’s called a “community arts center.”
And it’s happening on August 3rd and 4th.

Yeah, of this year, but so far we haven’t raised that much of the $200,000 necessary to rehabilitate because we’re gonna have to put a new staircase. I’m sorry you don’t have time to go by the station. It’s a beautiful gallery downstairs, which used to be the waiting room of the Long Island Railroad Station, and they’ve given us a five year lease with an honorary dollar a year leases courtesy of a good friend of mine who was the head of the MTA, the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, E. Virgil Conway. We got the station, so that’s what this festival is all about. That’s another hat I’m wearing out here in Montauk as president of that organization, and I’m retired, you know, so I’m only on tour with the Brothers [laughs].
Just a couple more questions and that’s it. And again, thank you for this great history.
Listen, I rap on and on and on, and I crossed over some of your questions. I apologize for that.
No, that’s okay. I could go on and on about my favorite MJQ recordings, the European concert collaboration and so forth, what is your favorite MJQ recording and why?

Yeah right [chuckles]. What do we got, fifty albums? I should have a favorite out of that? I don’t have the slightest idea of what would be my favorite. My favorite is the one I made the least mistakes on [laughs]. No, I’m just teasing, but there are some things that I’d rather not hear again, certain parts. Like they said at the time of the release, [there] were insignificant errors on my part, which didn’t completely destroy the whole composition. When you’re trying to improvise and do something different on the same compositions that you play every night, like “Django” and “Bags’ Groove,” we played every concert as encores, if not part of the program, for I couldn’t begin to say how many thousands of concerts we played. Those two compositions were mandatory, like “A- Train” for Duke Ellington, if he didn’t play “A-Train” or later “Satin Doll,” you could’ve stayed home ‘cause those were the things people wanted to hear. In order to play something different on those every time, one must take a chance. On some of the recordings, the professionalism is to be able to make a mistake and turn it into something, which comes with experience. Some of the young people may hesitate to be adventurous. Not so much on recordings, but on live performances, they should not hesitate to try something else that they hear in their head that might not come out that way with their fingers. This is the trick or what to try to seek with improvising, to be able to make a mistake and, like we used to say, “Like an artist, smear it over.” Jackson could do that. Jackson could hit one of those cracks, two notes accidentally, and turn it into something [snaps fingers] instantaneously, which come with years of trying. If you restrict yourself to play only what you know and what you’ve practiced or what you ran over, the instantaneous revelation of a musical idea, which comes while you’re playing, it’s a

beautiful thing to make it say what you heard. You hear all this music before you play it actually. It’s in your head before it comes to your fingers or in your chops. That’s what made people like Charlie Parker and Milt Jackson, the other great improvisers, the command of being able to hear it and do it. For the Quartet, every night, if we played the same compositions on a program, the tempo that it’s in that night dictates the ideas and the feeling of a piece at that time, just a slight change of tempo. Something John Lewis would do would throw Milt Jackson into doing something else, it’s really a beautiful thing to be part of and I was really fortunate to be in that, just as I feel now with my brothers. Tootie is [a] really phenomenal drummer, and I played all the drummers in jazz. I’m very comfortable with Tootie. He has that feeling and the ability to do whatever he thinks at the moment, too. And Jimmy too, but Jimmy is not as adventurous as he could be ‘cause we tried to get Jimmy to play just the three of us and he’s used to having either the guitar or the piano. He feels more comfortable with that. Like how you asked about Tony Purrone, who was involved in the Quintet for a long time. And we had uniforms like the MJQ, we had our little Cardin look-alikes and presented it that way, but now with this looser organization as far as no-uniforms, we come sharp but different. But I’m having a lot of fun with them, and we’re gonna have a lot of fun on this tribute to me. It’ll be the first time the Brothers played out here in a long time. I’m sorry you won’t be around for that. Bob Berg has consented to do it, and Chico Hamilton and his Euphoria, his latest group, and Eddie Locke and his group, and Jerry Sokolov and his group, and the Trio, it’s gonna be quite a long day of events. I hope it raises some money to rehabilitate that train [station], so we can have the workshops upstairs and the photo lab for kids. It’s a project in progress. That’s about what I’m doing now.
Final question, will there ever be a Percy Heath album? You’ve never recorded as a leader, and at this stage of the game, I think that’s a fair question.

I don’t know about a Percy Heath album. Those Heath Brothers’ albums are a collaboration. I have about ten compositions of mine. Maybe, one day. After the duets at the Lincoln Center with Jeb Patton, did you go to those?
I was out of town. I heard they were good though.

I was a little reluctant to do it in the first place, just me and a piano player? What the heck am I gonna do for two hours? But it turned out to be allright, so it’s possible that if some recording company wants to…
I think we can get some people interested [laughs].

Yeah, well we’ll see. It would take me quite a while to get enough together. I’d hate to have an album of repetitive licks. We’ll see if we can get it together. There’s a suite that I wrote on the passing of my father that has three movements to it. We did a couple of them separately on some of the Heath Brothers’ albums, but never as a suite. So now that I’m the survivor of the Modern Jazz Quartet, so many thoughts when I listen to

some of those recordings and bringing back those memories of those times when that happened and where we were and things we were doing for half a century, it’s… I don’t want to be too morbid about it, but there’s a part in the suite that expresses sadness, call it, “Lament,” and the other part, “Rejoice,” which should be the celebration of that passing. We’re working on it, Eugene, we’ll see what happens with that, if I’m around long enough to do that. Only time will tell. Thank you for including me in this study. Jimmy did it quite a few years ago, I understand. I was supposed to do it a couple of years ago, but they ran out of funds, which that wasn’t the reason why I consented to do it, but it’s just an honor to be included in this study of people who contributed to the art form that we have all dedicated our lives to. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Thank you very much.

segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview at Heath's Montauk home
segments.summary: Holley introduces the session at Percy Heath's home in Montauk on July 23, 2001; Heath jokes about the date and asks to be called Percy.

segments.title: Birth, parents and the Heath siblings' nicknames
segments.summary: Heath gives his full name, birth in Wilmington, NC in 1923, his parents, and his sister Elizabeth and brothers Jimmy and Tootie, whom their grandfather nicknamed.

segments.title: Meeting June, who brought Charlie Parker records, in 1947
segments.summary: Heath says he met his wife June Jones in Philadelphia in 1947; she managed a record store and brought him the latest bebop records.

segments.title: Buying a bass in 1946, Red Garland's jams and learning with Jimmy
segments.summary: Out of the service in 1946, Heath buys a bass, plays early jam sessions with Red Garland, practices while Jimmy learns piano, and becomes house bassist at the Downbeat where he meets June.

segments.title: No interracial marriage license in Pennsylvania; married in New York, 1950
segments.summary: The Heaths could not marry in Pennsylvania, so they went to New York in 1950; Heath describes his first trio with Bill Hollis and Harry Craft and getting his union card.

segments.title: The Downbeat house rhythm section and Jimmy's big band
segments.summary: Heath describes practicing, listening to Symphony Sid, the Philadelphia musicians at the Downbeat, headliners like Lockjaw Davis and Howard McGhee, and how Jimmy's big band fed Dizzy's.

segments.title: Playing the Ritz Bar in Wilmington, Delaware, and meeting Clifford Brown
segments.summary: Heath recalls commuting to Wilmington with the Hollis Hoppers, the segregation there, and a shy young Clifford Brown saying he would play jazz too.

segments.title: Bass lessons at Granoff and Dizzy's band at Mama's table, 1946
segments.summary: Heath took lessons from Mr. Quintelli and describes inviting Milt Jackson, John Lewis, Ray Brown and Kenny Clarke from Dizzy's band home for a family meal.

segments.title: Father Percy Sr.: Elks clarinetist and master mechanic
segments.summary: Heath describes his father's weekend clarinet in the Elks band and his thriving truck and car repair business in the late 1920s.

segments.title: The Depression, the NRA and WPA ruin Father's business
segments.summary: The National Recovery Act drove Percy Sr. out of business; the family went on WPA relief before he returned to work for a salary at the garage.

segments.title: Father's clarinet in the pawnshop and the Elks band
segments.summary: Percy Sr. pawned his clarinet during the week, redeemed it Saturdays for rehearsals with the Elks band, and the parents won an award in Atlantic City in 1937.

segments.title: Mother, Fat Mama, gospel singing and church life
segments.summary: Heath's mother sang in the choir, his Choctaw grandmother was devout, and he sang in a family gospel quartet and played violin; his father avoided church.

segments.title: Quitting the family garage job for the Pennsylvania Railroad
segments.summary: Asked about the Air Force, Heath instead describes leaving his father's employer over mistreatment and working at the Pennsylvania Railroad roundhouse as a laborer doing machinist's work.

segments.title: Segregated schools and growing up in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Heath describes institutional segregation in Philadelphia schools and playing in the street with Italian children.

segments.title: Rejected as 4F, then drafted and sent to aviation cadet training in 1943
segments.summary: Heath tried to volunteer as an aircraft mechanic, was classed 4F for being underweight, then was classed 1A when drafted and qualified for aviation cadet training.

segments.title: Keesler Field in Biloxi: tents, tests and calling cadence
segments.summary: Heath describes six months of testing and humiliating conditions at Keesler Field, being outspoken, and his earlier high school years in Wilmington.

segments.title: Tuskegee: college detachment, primary flight training and the air base
segments.summary: Heath describes learning wind vectors, flying small trainers and a Stearman, and moving to Tuskegee Army Air Field for the segregated training program.

segments.title: General B.O. Davis, the Tuskegee Airmen film and bracing upperclassmen
segments.summary: Heath comments on the accuracy of the Tuskegee Airmen movie, the hazing, soloing the AT-6 and receiving his commission and wings in January 1945.

segments.title: Walterboro: P-40s, P-47s and no combat
segments.summary: Heath describes transition training in South Carolina, mock dogfights with Marine pilots, and his unit's cancelled deployment as the war ended.

segments.title: Philadelphia as a proving ground compared with New York
segments.summary: Holley asks about Howard McGhee and the New York versus Philadelphia scenes; Heath calls Philadelphia a proving ground and Holley raises Coltrane.

segments.title: Coltrane on alto, then stranded in Chicago with Howard McGhee
segments.summary: Heath recalls Coltrane learning bebop in Jimmy's band, then the first road trip with McGhee to Chicago where the gangster owner paid with bad checks.

segments.title: The Chittlin' Circuit theater show with Sarah Vaughan and Illinois Jacquet
segments.summary: Heath describes playing the Apollo, Regal and Paradise theaters with McGhee's big band on a bill with Sarah Vaughan and Jacquet's band including John Lewis.

segments.title: John Lewis as an economical accompanist
segments.summary: Heath describes John Lewis's playing in Dizzy's band, his part on Two Bass Hit, and the early Milt Jackson quartet.

segments.title: Three Deuces, January 1948, and living in McGhee's Harlem apartment
segments.summary: Heath describes playing 52nd Street with McGhee's sextet and big band while living with Jimmy in McGhee's 115th Street walk-up, not having moved to New York.

segments.title: John Simmons and the Hawkins record that made him want to play bass
segments.summary: Asked about bassists he absorbed, Heath says he listened to anyone, but hearing John Simmons on a Coleman Hawkins record drew him to the bass.

segments.title: The 1948 Paris festival: playing with Hawkins and Kenny Clarke
segments.summary: Heath recalls the first international jazz festival in Paris with McGhee, and a matinee with Coleman Hawkins where he learned to listen to Kenny Clarke's cymbal.

segments.title: The MJQ future members at the Heath house in 1946; John Lewis and the chicken
segments.summary: Heath says he met John Lewis, Ray Brown and Milt Jackson at his mother's house, and tells how John Lewis silently refused the fried chicken in his fur coat.

segments.title: Joe Morris's rhythm and blues band with Philly Joe Jones and Johnny Griffin
segments.summary: Heath cannot place a Moody or Griffin album but recalls six months in 1948 with Joe Morris's R&B band and its personnel.

segments.title: Refused a sandwich in Wilmington after his Air Force service
segments.summary: On the road with Joe Morris in Wilmington, Delaware, Heath and bandmates were refused service at a counter, which made him question his service.

segments.chapter: Views on jazz, race and Europe
segments.title: Why Europe received jazz differently, and James Reese Europe
segments.summary: Heath says Europeans were more color-blind about the music than Americans, and credits James Reese Europe's military band in Paris with introducing swing.

segments.chapter: Views on jazz, race and Europe
segments.title: Professor Willis James at Lenox on the origins of the music
segments.summary: Heath recalls a lecture at the MJQ's school in Lenox tracing jazz rhythm to field hollers, banned drums and church handclaps.

segments.chapter: Views on jazz, race and Europe
segments.title: Why Latin and hyphenated jazz is not jazz to him
segments.summary: Heath disagrees with Dizzy that all world music will merge, insisting that jazz must keep its own rhythm.

segments.chapter: Views on jazz, race and Europe
segments.title: Growing up with the Victrola and the 'race music' record category
segments.summary: Heath explains that records by black artists were filed as race music, subdivided into gospel, blues, pop and jazz.

segments.chapter: Views on jazz, race and Europe
segments.title: Duke Ellington as role model and the MJQ's matching dress
segments.summary: Heath describes the presentation of Ellington-era bands, the MJQ's equal dress, and calls Milt Jackson the greatest improviser on his instrument.

segments.title: Leaving Philadelphia for New York after a police incident, 1949
segments.summary: Heath explains he met the headliners in Philadelphia jam sessions, and that a police remark to June after a movie convinced them to move to New York in 1949.

segments.title: Pneumonia, the union transfer card and June's hospital job, 1949
segments.summary: Heath describes working with Philly Joe, getting pneumonia, June working as a nurse's aide while his union transfer cleared, and living on Sugar Hill.

segments.title: Ten-dollar dance gigs and Birdland with Miles, Fats Navarro and Bud Powell
segments.summary: Heath describes early New York gigs with Sonny Rollins, Kenny Drew and Art Taylor, then Miles's Birdland band in 1950 and Fats Navarro's last gig.

segments.title: Rehearsing and recording with Mary Lou Williams
segments.summary: Heath recalls rehearsing with Mary Lou Williams and Julius Watkins and a forgotten trio record, and notes he joined Dizzy in 1950.

segments.title: The Smart Affairs revue with Milt Buckner and Charlie Fowlkes
segments.summary: Heath describes a revue band led by Milt Buckner with Tim Owens and baritonist Charlie Fowlkes, and a road trip that broke union rules.

segments.title: Dizzy's sextet with Coltrane, Milt Jackson and a parade of drummers
segments.summary: Heath recalls joining Dizzy in 1950-51 alongside Coltrane, who was fighting addiction, and the many drummers who came and went.

segments.title: Bud Powell living in Benny Harris's house
segments.summary: Heath tells how Oscar Goodstein asked him to get Bud Powell home from Birdland, and how June was nervous with Bud in the house.

segments.title: Percy's birth, Dizzy's nickname 'Spoons' and a Chicago hotel refusal
segments.summary: Heath missed his son's birth while on the road, Dizzy named him 'Spoons', and a Chicago hotel would not take the couple so they stayed at Johnny Griffin's grandmother's.

segments.title: Early records: Paris with McGhee, Dizzy's DG label and Kenny Burrell's first date
segments.summary: Heath looks back on his first recordings after a year and a half of playing, including Paris sessions, Bud Powell, and Dizzy's date with Joe Carroll.

segments.title: Leaving Dizzy over pay in 1951
segments.summary: Heath describes Dizzy's clowning on stage, the $115 weekly pay, and Dizzy telling him he was not worth it, which ended his time in the band.

segments.title: Monte Kay, Birdland and the mob-run New York clubs
segments.summary: Heath recalls meeting Monte Kay in 1952, the Levys' ownership of Birdland, and the double standard that kept Monk without a cabaret card.

segments.title: Monte Kay's Downbeat club and the Symphony Sid All-Stars
segments.summary: Heath describes the club on 54th Street, Earl May playing left-handed, and the Symphony Sid All-Stars with Miles, Kenny Clarke and J.J. Johnson.

segments.title: House bassist on Prestige and Blue Note dates, and gigs with Ben Webster
segments.summary: Heath explains he paid his rent by recording for Prestige and Blue Note with Art Farmer, Horace Silver and Milt Jackson, and mentions Ben Webster at Bowman's.

segments.title: Setting the record straight on Miles and Monk's supposed fight
segments.summary: Heath says the Monk and Miles fistfight story is false; Miles asked Monk to 'stroll' and Monk was hurt, nothing more.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: How the Milt Jackson Quartet began: the 'Milt Meets Sid' reunion date
segments.summary: Heath explains the quartet grew from Milt, John, Kenny and Percy and a late 1951 reunion date with Ray Brown while John studied at Manhattan School.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: John Lewis's plan, Mingus lessons and choosing the name Modern Jazz Quartet
segments.summary: John Lewis wanted to write new music and told Percy to improve; Heath asked Mingus for lessons and the group chose the name Modern Jazz Quartet.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Incorporating as the Modern Jazz Society and 'Milt Jackson and the MJQ' billing
segments.summary: Heath discusses the January 1952 incorporation, Harold Lovett's role, the billing of the first records, and why Kenny Clarke resisted written drum parts.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: John Lewis's master plan: concert stage and chamber music
segments.summary: Heath explains Lewis's concept of four lines in counterpoint, formal dress, and moving jazz out of smoky nightclubs.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Swinging Bach: improvisation inside the MJQ's written music
segments.summary: Heath says every MJQ piece swung and had improvisation, and that no two concerts had the same solos.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Never the same solo twice, unlike solos that became arrangements
segments.summary: Heath contrasts the MJQ's fresh improvisation with fixed solos like 'Flying Home' and 'Cotton Tail'.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Ray Brown's 'spider' fingering and Oscar Pettiford
segments.summary: Heath explains what Ray Brown showed him about hand position, why Oscar Pettiford was his idol, and that Pettiford wrote 'One Bass Hit'.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Tape change and resumption of the interview
segments.summary: Holley announces tape two and repeats the date, and Heath reminds him to include the year.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Mingus's fingering exercises, intonation and knowing where one is
segments.summary: Heath credits Mingus's exercises for his intonation, which he later taught at Lenox, and recalls Miles's remark about finding one.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Heath's concept of building a walking bass line
segments.summary: Heath explains Walter Page, strong and weak beats, and implying harmony while staying the foundation, plus John Lewis's role as teacher.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: John Lewis the teacher; soft playing in nightclubs; Milt's composing
segments.summary: Heath tells how Lewis answered a symphony player's quip, how the MJQ quieted talkative clubs, and how Lewis turned Milt's lines into songs.

segments.chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
segments.title: Milt Jackson's perfect pitch and photographic memory
segments.summary: Heath describes Milt recalling complicated fugues after a year's gap when John played a passage.

segments.title: The Club Chantilly: the first MJQ engagement
segments.summary: Heath recalls the first gig in Greenwich Village with tiny audiences, the first records, and the trip to play opposite Brubeck in 1955.

segments.title: Why Kenny Clarke left and what makes drummers swing
segments.summary: Heath says Kenny quit because he would not play written drum parts, and discusses swing among Clarke, Max Roach, Blakey and Connie Kay.

segments.title: The first MJQ bass solos: 'One Bass Hit', 'La Ronde' and Bachianas Brasileiras
segments.summary: Heath discusses carrying Dizzy's arrangement into the Quartet, composing his own line on 'La Ronde', and playing cello parts of Bachianas Brasileiras.

segments.title: Hip-hop sampling and childhood rapping
segments.summary: Told his La Ronde line was sampled by Branford Marsalis, Heath says hip-hop is like bebop and recalls rapping as a boy.

segments.title: Sideshow bands, families who discouraged jazz, and the MJQ's salary
segments.summary: Heath remembers his father taking the family to circus sideshow bands, notes many black families discouraged jazz, and says MJQ was exceptional at $600 a week.

segments.title: The MJQ's steady salary and moving the family to Montauk
segments.summary: Heath explains the group's salary, his insistence on summers at home with June and the three boys, and settling in Montauk from 1963.

segments.title: Connie Kay joins the MJQ for the Brubeck date in Washington
segments.summary: Heath recalls Art Blakey sitting in once, then Connie Kay joining and rehearsing on the train to Washington.

segments.title: Kenny Clarke after leaving: Annie Ross and the son
segments.summary: Heath recalls Kenny going back to Paris, his marriage to Annie Ross, their son Liaquat, and Carmen McRae.

segments.title: Connie Kay's Sonor kit, the Zildjian visits, and a bass with its own seat
segments.summary: Heath describes Connie's drum setup, cymbal choices, a forty-pound gong, 400 pounds of overweight, airline letters for the bass, and Kolstein.

segments.title: Donaueschingen 1957: morning clothes, Prince Fürstenberg and No Sun in Venice
segments.summary: Heath recalls the Quartet's 1957 festival in Germany, the old prince's dinner and tie pin, and playing the 'No Sun in Venice' funeral piece.

segments.title: Monte Kay, Pete Cameron and booking the MJQ into concert halls
segments.summary: Heath explains how Monte Kay and Pete Cameron booked classical series in Italy and Germany, the Weavers date, and Dick Gregory.

segments.title: Nesuhi Ertegun's hands-off Atlantic and rehearsing before recording
segments.summary: Heath says Atlantic let John Lewis do what he wanted and the MJQ rehearsed pieces for months so recording was like a gig.

segments.title: The 1956 Birdland All-Stars tour of Germany and France
segments.summary: Heath recalls touring by bus with Miles, Lester Young, Bud Powell and the Quartet, and the first search for a bass in Berlin.

segments.title: Buying the Rogeri bass in Berlin, 1956
segments.summary: Heath tells how Michelot found an old Rogeri-style bass, how he borrowed $1,000 from the Quartet, and its later restoration by Barry Kolstein.

segments.title: The 1957 tour: Donaueschingen's jazz ban and the arrival of free jazz
segments.summary: Heath says the Quartet overshadowed the festival so jazz was dropped, until free jazz arrived, and shares his view of free jazz.

segments.title: Miles Davis in later years: too loud, and his favorite Miles record
segments.summary: Heath recounts a Scandinavian festival where Miles's electric band was too loud, says he prefers the 'Walking' session, and recalls a flubbed set.

segments.title: The No Sun in Venice score, 'Three Windows' and The Comedy
segments.summary: Heath explains John Lewis's fugue linking the film themes, the Fontessa and Comedia dell'Arte pieces, and the Italian TV appearance in 1957.

segments.title: June at home with three boys during the long tours
segments.summary: Heath explains the 88-city tour, his promises to June, moving out of the middle-income project to Queens, and credits June.

segments.title: Connie Kay's family
segments.summary: Heath recalls Connie Kay's real name Kirnon, wife Addie, sons Rodney and Noel and second wife Frances.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: Odds Against Tomorrow and its racial theme
segments.summary: Heath contrasts No Sun in Venice with Odds Against Tomorrow, explaining the film's story about Belafonte and Robert Ryan and its message on prejudice.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: Bill Evans on the Odds Against Tomorrow soundtrack and other jazz film scores
segments.summary: Heath recalls Bill Evans's calliope part on 'Skating in Central Park' and mentions Miles and Ellington film work.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: The Lenox School of Jazz and the Music Barn
segments.summary: Heath describes the MJQ as artists-in-residence, the school's faculty, his student Larry Ridley, and why the school ended.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: Jazz at the Philharmonic and Norman Granz
segments.summary: Heath says Granz was unsure about John Lewis's concept, preferred jam-session style, and pressed Milt to play more.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: Did John Lewis hold Milt Jackson back?
segments.summary: Heath says Milt wanted straight bebop with a pumping rhythm section but the Quartet's setting made him stand out, and that Milt found leading a band hard.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: Why the MJQ broke up in 1974
segments.summary: Heath explains Milt quit after the Australian tour, wanting more money, and claimed he was threatened; Heath defends the group's pay.

segments.chapter: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
segments.title: 'Bubba' nickname, Milt's finances and the Pablo album
segments.summary: Heath tells how he and Milt began calling each other Bubba, Milt's money complaints, and the Pablo album required to release Milt.

segments.title: The MJQ regroups in 1981 after a Japan remark
segments.summary: Heath describes the final concerts, the Heath Brothers' Columbia albums, the Monterey in Japan tour, and a remark that led Tokyo Broadcasting to bring the Quartet back.

segments.title: Connie Kay's stroke, Mickey Roker, then Tootie Heath replaces him
segments.summary: Heath recalls Connie's stroke before a Hogwood Brandenburg concert in Boston, Mickey Roker joining, then Tootie taking the drum chair until Milt died.

segments.title: The last concert and the gap in the MJQ's history
segments.summary: Heath says the break was not as long as publicized, and describes Heath Brothers recordings on Columbia, Antilles and Concord.

segments.title: Against crossover: Mtume, Grover Washington and the 'beat back in jazz'
segments.summary: Heath explains why he told Jimmy a crossover piece would not work, rebukes a producer's claim about dancing, and says the MJQ never compromised.

segments.title: Third Stream, Gunther Schuller and the Beaux Arts album
segments.summary: Heath describes playing Schuller's atonal ballet piece with the New York City Ballet, his dislike of the 'Third Stream' label, and the Swedish orchestra album.

segments.title: Early television: Look Up and Live, What's My Line and Merv Griffin
segments.summary: Heath recalls MJQ appearances on TV shows in the 1950s and says he has tapes, while Holley notes missing TV in the biography.

segments.title: 'Home', the Today Show theme and MJQ Publishing
segments.summary: Heath explains that 'Home' used an old blues bass line and that its use as the Today Show theme in 1966 earned the group publishing royalties.

segments.title: Ralph Gleason's Jazz Casual and the Claxton photograph
segments.summary: Heath says Gleason was a big fan and helped arrange a Bill Claxton cover photo, and the restored tapes were not acceptable.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: The Beatles missing an MJQ concert and the Apple label
segments.summary: Heath recalls Royal Festival Hall black-market tickets that kept the young Beatles out, and how a friend of Monte Kay's got the Quartet on Apple.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Under the Jasmine Tree and John Lewis composing on tour
segments.summary: Heath describes John Lewis writing on a silent keyboard, and the film origin of 'Under the Jasmine Tree'.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Playing for heads of state: Nixon's State Dinner, the Shah and King Hassan II
segments.summary: Heath tells the story of the receiving line reversed by the Shah, Nixon's 'MJQs', June refusing to attend, the Kennedy Center, and King Hassan.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Space, the unreleased Kemek film score and Plastic Dreams
segments.summary: Heath discusses the Apple album Space, the Kemek film whose director died, and 'Plastic Dreams'.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: The Apple liner notes and the Plastic Dreams cover
segments.summary: Heath says he does not know who wrote the political liner notes or designed the risque Plastic Dreams cover.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Third tape begins and the 'modest home in paradise'
segments.summary: Holley announces tape three, and Heath jokes about the modest home in paradise.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Each member's duties: Lewis, Jackson, Kay and Heath as 'Minister of Finance'
segments.summary: Heath explains John Lewis as musical director, Milt as public relations, Connie as 'Minister of Transport' and Percy handling money.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Writing 'The Watergate Blues' and handing it to Ehrlichman
segments.summary: Heath explains why he wrote the song about Nixon and Ford's pardon, and recalls giving a copy to John Ehrlichman at a Boston TV show.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Origins of the Heath Brothers and the Columbia albums
segments.summary: Heath describes joining his brothers after the Quartet broke up and the four Columbia albums.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Strata-East and the 'Marchin' On' album with Stanley Cowell
segments.summary: Heath recalls the first Heath Brothers gig in Pescara, the Strata-East record with their parents on the cover, and his father's pride.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Stanley Cowell and the Heath Brothers' ups and downs
segments.summary: Heath mentions Stanley Cowell's upcoming concert, the Columbia and Island albums and the MJQ reforming.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Montauk Artists' Association, the train station and the Montauk Jazz Festival
segments.summary: Heath describes his current gigs and the fundraiser festival to rehabilitate the old train station as an arts center.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Favorite MJQ recording and turning mistakes into music
segments.summary: Heath says he has no favorite, discusses playing 'Django' and 'Bags' Groove' nightly, and says a good improviser can turn a mistake into something.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Hearing the idea first, playing with his brothers and the Montauk tribute
segments.summary: Heath explains hearing music before playing it, compares Tootie and Jimmy, and previews the Montauk tribute lineup.

segments.chapter: Apple, state occasions, roles and the Heath Brothers
segments.title: Will there be a Percy Heath album? Closing thanks
segments.summary: Heath says he might record a suite for his father with 'Lament' and 'Rejoice', and thanks Holley.
